taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Andropogon gerardi Vitman. The widespread North American spelling Andropogon gerardii is retained as a primary alias/search term because it remains standard in many Texas and U.S. references.
look_here_first: BIG BLUESTEM: a few (often 2–6) relatively STOUT, exposed terminal turkey-foot racemes that can be traced to ONE flowering culm. For detailed identification, the learner now shows Bob Harms's actual Central Texas measured flowering-unit/spikelet and sheath images alongside two Matt Lavin membranous-ligule photos. Study REAL awned fertile sessile and pedicelled companion grass flowers, rachis hairs and their disarticulation—but don't call the tiny individual organ arrows resolved until a same-specimen attachment is inspected. Florida paspalum, also native, can mimic sterile big: big often has a bronze INNER SHEATH and a blade narrowing near collar; Florida tends GREEN inner sheath and more uniform blade width, while BOTH may have BROWN or jagged MEMBRANOUS LIGULES. These supporting differences need two opened live sheaths in matching photographs. KR is introduced, little bluestem and Indiangrass native; full branch origin beats color or 3-finger-only guesses.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays County Ranch native tallgrass documentation; Texas Conservation Action Plan Travis County Blackland Prairie community documentation; NPSOT Williamson County locally sourced historic prairie seed provenance.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: All three counties are explicitly named by project-acceptable sources; no broad prairie-range inference.

best_field_traits: Tall warm-season perennial with robust upright stems from a persistent crown or short rhizomes.
Typically 2–6 relatively stout exposed racemes radiating near the culm tip; commonly three suggest a turkey-foot.
Leaf blades commonly broader than little bluestem; collar often hairy, with a short chiefly membranous ligule.
Paired sessile/pedicelled spikelets along racemes, with awns; inspect with a lens for confirmation.
Not the many SHORT separately sheathed racemes of little bluestem or the brushy plume of bushy bluestem.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Follow branching, not autumn color. BIG: a few fairly stout, exposed racemes radiate near one culm tip. LITTLE: many short, silky racemes distributed on separate upper leafy branches. KR: multiple finer slender racemes in a clustered head can resemble BIG; count alone is not proof, so inspect attachment, leaf collar and mature spikelets. INDIANGRASS: one plume-like panicle rather than a true turkey-foot.
morphology_keys.photo_specific_evidence: The existing file 01-whole-plant.jpg is actually a leaf-collar/ligule macro; files 02 and 03 show multiple grasses and general habitat, not species-isolated diagnostic seedheads. Source descriptions and original thumbnails were inspected 2026-10-21. Do not use those three image filenames as evidence of the old roles.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Big bluestem: usually 2–6 exposed relatively stout racemes close together at the terminal head (often a turkey-foot). Little bluestem: many short silky racemes repeated on separate leafy upper branchlets. KR bluestem: long thin clustered terminal racemes, often overlapping in count, so use several characters rather than seedhead count alone. Bushy bluestem: bulky fuzzy plume. Broomsedge: narrower silky flowering units subtended by spathe-like sheaths. Indiangrass: elongated single plume-like inflorescence.

curation_status.latest_review_note: Source image 01 = membranous ligule; 02/03 = mixed grass scenes. Two taxon-specific anatomy references added to visual comparison, with checked gross-structure arrows. Specialized local full head + paired spikelets still missing.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_memory_rule: BIG = usually a few stout racemes near ONE terminal branching point. LITTLE = numerous short hairy racemes on multiple separate upper leafy axes; KR = finer terminal radiating racemes, count overlapping. On nonflowering shoots use paired sheath/blade characters cautiously.
field_id_finish_pass.look_here_first: Follow a complete flowering stem to the top. Look for several stout spikes projecting from near one point; photograph their common branching center before counting fingers.
field_sequence: Photograph a rooted mature culm from crown to upper seedhead, including the actual head branching point.
Count and TRACE exposed racemes: big bluestem often has 2–6 near the tip, usually thicker than KR, but their ranges overlap.
Inspect the same plant's leaf collar. A short chiefly membranous ligule and hairs around the collar support big bluestem; the approved Lavin image shows the ligule well.
Use a hand lens on attached sessile and pedicelled spikelets and awns; compare with verified KR bluestem, little bluestem, and Indiangrass.
If only a mixed-species prairie photo or vegetative shoot is available, record Andropogoneae / bluestem sp. rather than forcing a species.
important_cautions: Three-tipped turkey-foot is common but not mandatory: two to six exposed racemes can be present.
The old three-photo gallery was incorrectly labelled. Its existing whole-plant file is a collar macro; its other two files contain mixed grasses.
The external two macro views are from Montana, not Hays County; original labels and licenses are preserved.
No arrow is placed on a doubtful grass in the mixed-species photos.
Do not change the already reviewed Hays County native-range status from this photography audit.

Florida paspalum's MEMBRANOUS LIGULE can be brown (USGS 1.2–3.3 mm); the inner SHEATH tends green in USGS's big-vs-Florida description. Do not teach green ligule as Florida or bronze ligule as big. Tapers and pigment vary; need matching photos.

Bob Harms locally focused educational-use exact species photos with printed scale bars are now linked in big bluestem's public photo gallery, but no claim of individually vouchered Hays specimen or verified 1mm segmented ruler unit. Photographer retains copyright; use educational with credit only.

lookalike_quick_key.cue: Short hairy racemes distributed through multiple upper leafy branches, not a few long exposed terminal fingers.
Introduced KR: typically several longer thinner fingerlike racemes gathered at the head; inspect collars/spikelets because count and outline overlap.
Bushy bluestem: dense brushy plume of crowded silky racemes instead of open turkey-foot branches.
Broomsedge: slender silky racemes associated with conspicuous spathe-like sheaths; not broad open fingers.
Indiangrass: solitary elongated plumelike panicle; not a digitate set of several fingers.

crew_walkthrough: 1. TEXAS flowering architecture: inspect the separate Pedernales flowering culms and trace each terminal head to its own raceme junction; do not borrow racemes from neighboring culms.
2. Actual leaf collar: inspect Matt Lavin's existing photographed membranous ligule and hair fringe at the blade-sheath junction, recognizing these are NOT whole-plant pixels.
3. Live flowering detail: examine yellow anthers hanging from the purplish spikelet-bearing racemes in the newly sourced 2009 image.
4. Mature flowering close-up: inspect previously recorded actual big bluestem bent awn and spikelet region, acknowledging the lack of mm scale.
5. Look-alikes: compare verified little bluestem racemes on multiple leafy axes; narrow KR fingers; and the single long Indiangrass panicle.
6. Teach-back: point to a SINGLE plant's terminal branch attachment, membranous collar and fertile awned spikelet before asserting big bluestem.

big_final_morphology_crosscheck_20261022.botanical_correction: The paired pedicellate companion in big bluestem is commonly well developed and staminate, roughly approaching the 5–11 mm sessile unit; DO NOT teach it as the tiny reduced pedicel of little bluestem. Sessile spikelet carries the fertile upper floret and often bent/twisted awn; lower floret sterile. See FNA and Texas Flora.

fna_literature_measurements_NOT_PIXEL_ME.ligule_mm: 0.4–2.5 mm (Flora of North America treatment of typical big bluestem); conspicuous collar hairs can be present, but are not the true membranous ligule
fna_literature_measurements_NOT_PIXEL_ME.sessile_spikelet_mm: 5–11 mm; FNA reports awns 8–25 mm and usually well-developed staminate pedicellate spikelets 3.5–12 mm
fna_literature_measurements_NOT_PIXEL_ME.terminal_racemes: Typically 2–6(10) branches, often three, but finger count is not reliable alone
fna_literature_measurements_NOT_PIXEL_ME.note: Published descriptive ranges ONLY; no assumption any photographed individual has exactly these measurements.

field_teachback_four_checks: Trace one real mature big bluestem culm from base to actual terminal raceme insertion: do not group adjacent culms into one turkey foot.

Look at true leaf sheath INSIDE surface, not solely ligule color. Big often bronze inner sheath and lower blade narrowing near collar; Florida paspalum often GREEN inner sheath and more constant lower blade width. Both can have BROWN membranous ligules.

Follow one true purple raceme with hand lens: identify sessile fertile and WELL-DEVELOPED pedicellate usually male spikelets, then awn and hairy rachis. Preserve uncertainty until actual 1-mm same-sample image is available.

Compare flowering HEADS: big robust terminal 2–6 divergent racemes; little short separate upper axillary racemes; KR slimmer clustered terminals; Indiangrass single compound feathery panicle. Never base native removal decision on count alone.

items.label: NO FLOWERS? Florida paspalum (DIFFERENT species): flowering habit comparison
items.image_role: Large leafy erect grass clump with stiff flowering stalks among lush foliage
items.caption: PHOTO: Florida paspalum, NOT big bluestem. This licensed full-plant flowering image shows a different grass with stalks and leaves. At the blade/sheath junction use a fresh specimen: USGS notes big-bluestem blades narrow slightly near the collar and widen along the middle, often bronze cast on the inside of the sheath; Florida paspalum blades tend to maintain a steadier width and the inner sheath is typically green. THESE FINE COLOR/WIDTH FEATURES ARE NOT proven by this distant photo and no arrow is placed.
items.why_it_matters: A much-needed CREW vegetative look-alike for the season before big bluestem develops a turkey-foot. Do not identify only by blade shape, sheath color, or one habit picture.
items.creator: Sesamehoneytart
items.photo_status: Existing source-attributed physically saved photographic file; visible structure was inspected directly on 2026-10-20. Source taxon ID provisional; no unobserved or measured microscopic traits represented. Reused CC BY-SA 3.0 source-labelled other-species image physically archived in Paspalum floridanum canonical package; no close leaf/sheath pixels or false arrows.

items.label: LITTLE BLUESTEM (OTHER native species): distributed SHORT silky upper racemes
items.image_role: Source-labelled Montana wild-type little bluestem, close-up of flowering branches bearing distinct short silky racemes and subtending sheaths
items.caption: Different native grass: many SHORT white-silky racemes emerge from different leafy UPPER BRANCHES, unlike big bluestem's few longer stout terminal turkey-foot racemes. The visible branches matter more than red/brown color.
items.why_it_matters: A source-verified native species comparison helps avoid confusing two valuable prairie grasses.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Exact 960×1280 Wikimedia thumbnail viewed and licensed source file checked 2026-10-21; photo from Montana; original label Andropogon scoparius is accepted synonym of Schizachyrium scoparium; visible gross arrows only, not microscopy. SOURCE-CREDITED OTHER species comparison in big bluestem lesson; original author and arrows retained.

items.label: INTRODUCED KR BLUESTEM: more slender long terminal racemes
items.image_role: Actual archived source-labelled photo, several long flowering branches spreading from clustered lower portion
items.caption: Introduced Bothriochloa ischaemum. The three fingerlike RACEMES are narrow and converge near the top; big bluestem's are typically relatively stout but lengths and counts overlap. Use collar/spikelet confirmation, not only finger count or color.
items.why_it_matters: This Texas comparison focuses on the single-stem shared terminal attachment; user crew should verify native big before acting on suspected KR.
items.creator: Sam Kieschnick

items.label: INDIANGRASS (OTHER native species): ONE BRANCHED panicle
items.image_role: Independent taxon-labelled fall panicle field reference
items.caption: Indiangrass has a single elongated branched flowering plume and characteristic collar structure; it does not produce a set of a few stout exposed terminal racemes like big bluestem. This source image shows head architecture, not measured individual pedicels.
items.why_it_matters: Separates two flagship prairie grasses likely to grow together; leaves alone overlap and require collar detail.

visual_comparison.overlay_note:
Originals © Matt Lavin, CC BY-SA 2.0. Overlay arrows/annotations added for Glass Root Garden educational learner; source and reuse/license links retained. External reference files not counted among the three physically installed canonical photos.
New 2026-10-22 Matt Lavin images are genuine licensed photos of documented flowers/flowering heads, but not same-voucher, same-local-individual photomacro confirmation. PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING. Existing older structural arrows remain unchanged; no arrows added for uncertain sub-millimeter structures. Detailed second-pass follow-on 2026-10-22: four other-species exact-source photo comparisons added with credits/licensing preserved, including normally-overlooked vegetative Florida paspalum; original five big photos retained, scientific/photo holds unchanged. No collar-margin or leaf-blade supporting feature marked without real pixels. Added Matt Lavin Commons CC BY-SA 2.0 exact species photo captioned 'ligule is a lacerated membrane' with NO speculative arrows. Do not treat membrane as fringe hairs or assume Florida paspalum has a GREEN ligule (USGS explicitly says P. floridanum ligule BROWN, 1.2–3.3mm); the historical comparison is big INNER SHEATH often bronze versus Florida green. Added five exact source-image Bob Harms Selected Central Texas Monocots (ANGE-i,j1,L,9,d) from original HTML links, photographed pixels reviewed. Images include scale bars, original rights are EDUCATIONAL permission (NOT CC). NO unsafe guess-level anatomy arrows or new physical JPEGs. No changes to existing photos or historic native taxonomy holds.

photo_sequence.heading: WHOLE ROOTED BIG BLUESTEM
photo_sequence.teach: A real single native Hays County mature clump must show stem base, perennial shoots, lower leaves and full head in same sequence. Old archived files 02/03 are mixed species and are NOT this proof.

photo_sequence.heading: TEXAS FLOWERING HEADS
photo_sequence.status: REAL SOURCE PHOTO — TEXAS; rooted same-stem not proved
photo_sequence.teach: Find ONE flowering head in the Pedernales Matt Lavin photo, trace only its own 2–6 exposed sturdy terminal racemes to their convergence; don't add fingers from nearby grasses.

photo_sequence.heading: LOCAL SOURCE — MAGNIFIED FLOWERING BRANCH
photo_sequence.status: REAL BOB HARMS CENTRAL TEXAS PHOTO WITH VISIBLE SCALE
photo_sequence.teach: Observe an entire awned flowering BRANCH, source-labelled Andropogon gerardii, and read its graduated reference. This is ONE raceme, not the full turkey-foot at shared stem tip.

photo_sequence.heading: LOCAL SOURCE — MAGNIFIED ATTACHED PAIRED UNITS
photo_sequence.status: REAL BOB HARMS REGIONAL CLOSEUP WITH SCALE; exact microscopic arrows pending
photo_sequence.teach: See paired flower-bearing units attached to their true rachis and awned lemmas. Do not assign sessile versus pedicelled companions to individual pixels until leaf-plane dissection is validated.

photo_sequence.heading: ACTUAL COLLAR AND LIGULE
photo_sequence.teach: The actual source-labelled Matt Lavin close-up shows a short predominantly membranous ligule with nearby hair fringe. The archived filename 01-whole-plant.jpg is MISLEADING: it is NOT a full plant. Measure true membrane, fringe, blade and sheath separately in fresh local specimen.

photo_sequence.heading: SECOND VIEW: LACERATE LIGULE EDGE
photo_sequence.status: NEW EXACT-SPECIES CC BY-SA SOURCE-LINKED MACRO — NO MILLIMETER SCALE
photo_sequence.teach: This other Matt Lavin photo actually shows the torn/tattered margin of BIG bluestem's membranous ligule. Compare membrane tissue with loose collar hairs. Both big bluestem and Florida paspalum may have a brown, lacerate-toothed membrane; color/height overlap and are NOT safe binary keys.

photo_sequence.heading: LOCAL SOURCE — OPEN DRIED SHEATH/LIGULE TISSUE
photo_sequence.status: REAL REGIONAL MICRO PHOTO WITH REFERENCE SCALE; membrane edge not individually arrowed
photo_sequence.teach: Compare Bob Harms's enlarged dry sheath/ligule tissue with TWO already licensed Matt Lavin photographs of the real membranous edge. DO NOT assume dry brown tissue is a vegetative big-versus-Florida color trait.

photo_sequence.heading: YELLOW ANTHERS WHEN FLOWERING
photo_sequence.teach: See hanging pollen-bearing yellow anthers from purple spikelet-bearing racemes. Do not confuse the anthers with mature awns, mature fruits or bristles.

photo_sequence.heading: STOUT SPIKELET-BEARING RACEMES
photo_sequence.teach: Learn the individual thicker spikelet-bearing units; full attachment of all racemes is out of frame so do not mark a common base here.

photo_sequence.heading: SESSILE SPIKELET + PEDICELLED PARTNER
photo_sequence.status: GROSS CLOSEUP PRESENT; MM-DISSECTION PHOTO GAP
photo_sequence.teach: There is a real bent awn and spikelet region. Isolate a mature attached 10–20× unit to label sessile fertile vs pedicellate partner, glumes, hairy rachis and point of actual awn origin, with a millimeter ruler.

photo_sequence.heading: LOCAL SOURCE — SEPARATED MATURE AWNED SPIKELETS
photo_sequence.status: REAL REGIONAL SCALED MACRO; exact paired attachment missing
photo_sequence.teach: Examine enlarged actual mature spikelets, glumes and long bent awns with the photographer's reference bar. It doesn't demonstrate which individual detached spikelet was the sessile fertile member on the original culm.

photo_sequence.heading: LOCAL SOURCE — DISARTICULATING HAIRY FLOWERING AXIS
photo_sequence.teach: Observe real pieces of rachis, long awns and silky pedicel/axis hairs. Hairs can be on the axis or stalk, not simply on 'seeds'. Do not label a fracture/attached pedicel without proof.

photo_sequence.heading: NO SEEDHEAD — FLORIDA PASPALUM
photo_sequence.status: CORRECT OTHER-SPECIES PHOTO, LEAF MICRO PAIR MISSING
photo_sequence.teach: Compare 2 correctly determined OPENED fresh sheaths and genuine blade bases. USGS describes BIG blades commonly narrowing close to the collar and often bronze INNER sheath surface, versus more uniformly wide lower blades and GREEN inner sheath surface on Florida paspalum. But BOTH have a membranous ligule, and Florida's ligule is often BROWN (USGS 1.2–3.3 mm), NOT reliably green. Color and blade taper are supporting characters only. No photo currently demonstrates both inners at matching scale; no invented arrows.

photo_sequence.heading: NATIVE LITTLE BLUESTEM
photo_sequence.teach: Many short silvery racemes spread along multiple separate upper leafy branches, not one turkey foot at the tip.

photo_sequence.heading: KR BLUESTEM (INTRODUCED)
photo_sequence.teach: Several slender long fingers converging at terminal head; character overlap, collar and pair macro essential before a removal decision.

photo_sequence.heading: INDIANGRASS
photo_sequence.teach: ONE elongated branched panicle with a characteristic exposed membranous rifle-sight collar (in Indiangrass's own species lesson), NOT a set of digitate exposed racemes.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Big bluestem — trace a whole flowering head to the actual spikelet anatomy
steps: START WITH THE REAL TEXAS HEAD (photo 4): trace the flowering stem into separate terminal racemes. This is not a rooted whole plant, and 'turkey foot' shape varies.
FOLLOW A SINGLE RACEME (photo 6): Bob Harms' credited Central Texas photograph shows a flowering branch, not a multi-raceme terminal head. Keep those views distinct.
READ THE SOURCE SCALE (photo 7): compare attached flowering units in the Harms regional image. Don't label sessile versus pedicellate partners by guessing which tiny part an arrow crosses.

OPEN THE INNER LEAF COLLAR (photos 1 and 8): examine the archived Matt Lavin actual membranous ligule and Harms' independent scaled sheath-region view; do not confuse bronze inner sheath with ligule color.

STUDY A DETACHED AWNED SPIKELET AND RACHIS FRAGMENT (photos 9–10): the two Harms images demonstrate separated reproductive material and disarticulation, but are not matched to a living local whole plant.

MATCH LOOK-ALIKES at the same flowering stage: little bluestem carries separated upper silky racemes; KR bluestem has a different fine terminal branching appearance; Indiangrass is one branched plume. Nonflowering Florida paspalum needs a matched split sheath/leaf comparison, not ligule color alone.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Trace the complete terminal flowering branches, corroborate with a real membranous collar/ligule and attached paired flowering units; do not certify by height, turkey-foot silhouette, or sheath color alone.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: 10 actual stored species JPEGs verified; 15 gallery panels include some EXTERNAL photos and DIFFERENT species comparisons. Several Harms images carry source-limited attributed educational permission, not Creative Commons. No new photos or microscopic arrows installed in this Lane 1 pass; 100% remains held.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FOLLOW ONE TURKEY-FOOT STEM
field_id_short_tiles.short: Trace 2–6(10) relatively stout exposed terminal racemes back to ONE culm; often three, never a required count.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Photograph the complete junction, not neighboring culms crossing in a prairie scene. Source images in panels 1 and 8 illustrate terminal branching and awned racemes but neither is a vouchered rooted Hays plant. Big bluestem is a robust perennial; head shape is a first clue, not a final determination.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING-HEAD PHOTOS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SAME ROOTED LOCAL CULM

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR — TRUE LIGULE, NOT SHEATH COLOR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Membranous ligule about 0.4–2.5 mm; collar hairs may surround it but are separate structures.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 4–6 contain actual source-labeled ligule/sheath views. Open the inner blade–sheath junction and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm bar on a single identified flowering stem. Florida paspalum may also have a brown or jagged membranous ligule; compare INNER sheath (often bronze in big, greener in Florida) and lower blade taper only with matched living material. Do not make a species ID from pigment alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE LIGULE PHOTO PRESENT — SAME-PLANT MEASUREMENT AND FLORIDA PAIR MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · PAIRED SPIKELETS — SESSILE AND PEDICELLED
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile spikelet about 5–11 mm; pedicelled companion often well developed, staminate, about 3.5–12 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: On one attached flowering branch locate the sessile fertile unit and its stalked companion. The companion is NOT automatically a tiny vestige: it is often a substantial pollen-bearing spikelet in big bluestem. Panels 2–3 and 9–11 show genuine reproductive source material, but no image proves a complete matched living Hays plant and dissection. Count and measure intact pairs with a millimeter scale.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE ANATOMY PHOTOS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SAME-VOUCHER ATTACHED PAIR

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMA AND BENT AWN — DO NOT SWAP LABELS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two glumes enclose the sessile unit; the upper fertile lemma carries a twisted, bent awn commonly about 8–25 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: A typical fertile sessile spikelet contains a lower sterile floret and an upper fertile floret. The glumes are NOT the awn-bearing fertile lemma: isolate each on the SAME tagged mature pair before placing arrows. Go Botany records two glumes per spikelet and glumes up to ~11 mm; a regional Missouri description gives lemma body ~5–9 mm, but do not substitute those published ranges for measurements of these photos. Kew treats the awn as arising from the notch/sinus of a two-lobed fertile lemma. Panels 3, 9 and 10 are teaching references, not independently verified organ-level arrow coordinates.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTED SAME-PAIR GLUMES/LEMMA/AWN

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — BIG, LITTLE, KR AND FLORIDA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Big has stout terminal fingers; little has many short upper axillary racemes; KR has finer clustered terminal fingers; Indiangrass has one branched plume.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 12–15 show DIFFERENT species, not big bluestem. KR bluestem is introduced and can overlap in raceme count, so compare the true collar and mature spikelet pairs before management decisions. Florida paspalum is a native vegetative look-alike; its greener inner sheath and less-tapered blade base are supporting tendencies, not absolute diagnostic rules. Bushy bluestem and broomsedge have more sheathed, fluffy flowering architecture. If evidence conflicts, record bluestem sp. or Andropogoneae rather than remove a presumed invasive.
field_id_short_tiles.status: EXISTING LOOK-ALIKE PANELS — SAME-ANGLE FIELD COMPARISON PENDING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO PRECISE HANDOFFS
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: 10 existing species image records and 15 teaching panels, but decisive connected anatomy and rights/site QA remain open.
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): one voucher-linked rooted Hays-area flowering culm with intact 2–6(10)-raceme terminal junction; the SAME plant's true ligule with 1-mm ruler; a mature attached sessile/pedicelled pair with separated glumes, ~5–9 mm fertile lemma and actual awn insertion at 10–20×; paired fresh split inner sheaths of big bluestem and Florida paspalum. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify all ten archived image files, 15 teaching panels, authors and image-level rights (especially five Bob Harms educational-only NOT-CC originals), existing arrows against pixels, other-species labels, six-tile mobile rendering, and rights-filtered public page. No new photos, arrows or Pages publication in this run. Preserve all county/taxonomy holds and remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until anatomical, license and display checks pass.
